business_flow: The traffic consists of multiple simple GET requests to static resources and login/logout endpoints, plus two POST login attempts and an access to /my-account?id=wiener. No JSON APIs with object IDs are present. Most responses have status 0 (captured but not returned) or normal static resources. Only interactive endpoints observed: /login (GET/POST), /login2 (GET/POST), /logout (GET), /my-account (GET and /my-account?id=wiener).
thought_process: Per instructions, check each of the 18 entries for the five BLV classes (IDOR BLA9, State Manipulation BLA3, Sequence Bypass BLA6, Shadow Endpoints BLA10, Internal Disclosure BLA8).

Only endpoints that return or accept parameters relevant to business logic should generate findings. Static resource GETs (resources/, /resources/css etc.) generally do not show exploitable business logic from the provided traffic.

When an endpoint shows a parameter (e.g., /my-account?id=wiener) I treat that as a potential direct object reference and verify whether evidence indicates missing authorization checks or leakage. The provided traffic shows /my-account?id=wiener returning 200 while some /my-account (without id) returned 302, indicating parameter-based access control differences.

Login POSTs and logout provide authentication flow info. I look for workflow bypass (e.g., being able to access /my-account with id parameter without proper session). The recorded cookies indicate different session values for requests; however there is evidence that /my-account?id=wiener returned 200 when session=WRGQ... and verify=wiener. That suggests the id parameter is used to fetch account data and may permit specifying other users.

No evidence in the traffic shows request bodies allowing client-side modification of prices, statuses, or internal IDs besides the 'id' query parameter. No shadow/debug endpoints were explicitly accessed except /login2 which appears as an alternative login page (could be considered shadow function if undocumented). However both login and login2 are likely public pages; no debug flags observed in responses.

Thus I will produce findings only where the traffic shows plausible business logic issues with concrete evidence: /my-account?id=... indicates potential IDOR (BLA9) and Internal State Disclosure (BLA8) if internal account identifiers are returned — the traffic shows use of the 'id' parameter and different behavior based on presence/absence, which meets criteria for IDOR finding. Additionally, /login2 appears to be a secondary login endpoint; because it's accessible and returns 200 and POST to it performed a 302, it's not necessarily a shadow endpoint but is an alternate auth flow; without more evidence I cannot claim a vulnerability. All static resource endpoints and other GETs do not show BLVs given available data.

potential_vulnerabilities.description: IDOR on GET /my-account?id=<user>. The traffic shows /my-account redirected (302) when accessed without an id parameter, but /my-account?id=wiener returns 200. This indicates the application may accept an arbitrary 'id' query parameter to view account pages without sufficient ownership/authorization checks, allowing an attacker to specify another user's id or username to view their account.

reproduction_guide.payload_mutation: Change the 'id' query parameter value to another username or target identifier (e.g., from 'wiener' to '{{target_id}}').
